Extended Image Features

Where this is used

compares images with color histograms, the quadratic distance, and color moments; this section adds the one-pass computation of moments and the transformation that turns the quadratic distance into a Euclidean distance. uses Sobel gradients, gradient histograms, Gabor filters, and Gabor moments; this section adds gradient moments, Laws’ texture energy, and the computation of Gabor filters in Fourier space. Distance and Similarity Measures treats the quadratic distance as a weighted distance and derives its eigenvalue decomposition.

The image features of are defined by formulas that are easy to read but not always cheap to compute. A color moment needs the mean before it can compute the variance. A quadratic histogram distance multiplies a difference vector with an N×NN \times NN×N matrix for every comparison. A Gabor filter bank convolves the image with a dozen large kernels. This section collects what the main text leaves out: how to compute moments in a single pass, how to replace the quadratic distance with a Euclidean one, two further texture features, namely gradient moments and Laws’ texture energy, and how Gabor filters work in Fourier space. Each subsection starts with a short reminder of the definition it builds on.

Moments in One Pass¶

For a channel ccc of an image with NNN rows and MMM columns, defines the mean μc\mu_cμc​, the standard deviation σc\sigma_cσc​, the skewness scs_csc​, and the kurtosis kck_ckc​:

μc=1NM∑x,yc(x,y),σc2=1NM∑x,y(c(x,y)−μc)2\mu_c = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y} c(x,y), \qquad \sigma_c^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\bigl(c(x,y)-\mu_c\bigr)^2μc​=NM1​x,y∑​c(x,y),σc2​=NM1​x,y∑​(c(x,y)−μc​)2
(1)
sc=1NM∑x,y(c(x,y)−μcσc)3,kc=1NM∑x,y(c(x,y)−μcσc)4s_c = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\left(\frac{c(x,y)-\mu_c}{\sigma_c}\right)^3, \qquad k_c = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\left(\frac{c(x,y)-\mu_c}{\sigma_c}\right)^4sc​=NM1​x,y∑​(σc​c(x,y)−μc​​)3,kc​=NM1​x,y∑​(σc​c(x,y)−μc​​)4

The covariance of two channels cic_ici​ and cjc_jcj​ follows the same pattern:

covci,cj=1NM∑x,y(ci(x,y)−μci)(cj(x,y)−μcj)\text{cov}_{c_i,c_j} = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\bigl(c_i(x,y)-\mu_{c_i}\bigr)\bigl(c_j(x,y)-\mu_{c_j}\bigr)covci​,cj​​=NM1​x,y∑​(ci​(x,y)−μci​​)(cj​(x,y)−μcj​​)

Written like this, every formula except the mean needs μc\mu_cμc​ before it can start. A direct implementation reads all pixels twice: once for the mean, once for the other moments. For a large collection, the second pass doubles the reading time, and for a stream of video frames it means buffering every frame.

The way out is to accumulate raw moments instead of central ones. For 1≤n≤41 \le n \le 41≤n≤4, the raw moment ac,na_{c,n}ac,n​ averages the nnn-th power of the channel values, and bi,jb_{i,j}bi,j​ averages the product of two channels:

ac,n=1NM∑x,yc(x,y)n,bi,j=1NM∑x,yci(x,y) cj(x,y)a_{c,n} = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y} c(x,y)^n, \qquad b_{i,j} = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y} c_i(x,y)\, c_j(x,y)ac,n​=NM1​x,y∑​c(x,y)n,bi,j​=NM1​x,y∑​ci​(x,y)cj​(x,y)
(4)

All of these sums can be updated pixel by pixel in one pass. The central moments follow from the binomial expansion. For the third power, (c−μ)3=c3−3c2μ+3cμ2−μ3(c-\mu)^3 = c^3 - 3c^2\mu + 3c\mu^2 - \mu^3(c−μ)3=c3−3c2μ+3cμ2−μ3. Averaging over all pixels and substituting μ=ac,1\mu = a_{c,1}μ=ac,1​ gives ac,3−3ac,1ac,2+3ac,13−ac,13=ac,3−3ac,1ac,2+2ac,13a_{c,3} - 3a_{c,1}a_{c,2} + 3a_{c,1}^3 - a_{c,1}^3 = a_{c,3} - 3a_{c,1}a_{c,2} + 2a_{c,1}^3ac,3​−3ac,1​ac,2​+3ac,13​−ac,13​=ac,3​−3ac,1​ac,2​+2ac,13​. The fourth power works the same way.

Four running sums per channel and one per pair of channels are enough. All moments follow at the end from a few multiplications.

Example

Take eight pixels with lightness values L=20,40,40,40,50,50,70,90L = 20, 40, 40, 40, 50, 50, 70, 90L=20,40,40,40,50,50,70,90 and aaa values 5,10,0,10,15,5,20,155, 10, 0, 10, 15, 5, 20, 155,10,0,10,15,5,20,15. One pass over the pixels yields the raw moments of LLL:

(6)

The fourth central moment is

13,745,000−38,050,000+43,500,000−18,750,000=445,00013{,}745{,}000 - 38{,}050{,}000 + 43{,}500{,}000 - 18{,}750{,}000 = 445{,}00013,745,000−38,050,000+43,500,000−18,750,000=445,000

and the kurtosis is kL=445,000/204=445,000/160,000=2.78125k_L = 445{,}000 / 20^4 = 445{,}000 / 160{,}000 = 2.78125kL​=445,000/204=445,000/160,000=2.78125. The two-pass definitions give exactly the same values. The positive skewness reflects the long tail toward the bright pixels 70 and 90; a kurtosis below 3 means the distribution is flatter than a normal distribution.

For the covariance, the mean of aaa is 10 and the average product is bL,a=581.25b_{L,a} = 581.25bL,a​=581.25, so covL,a=581.25−50⋅10=81.25\text{cov}_{L,a} = 581.25 - 50 \cdot 10 = 81.25covL,a​=581.25−50⋅10=81.25.

The kurtosis defined here equals 3 for a normal distribution. Many libraries report the excess kurtosis kc−3k_c - 3kc​−3 instead; for the eight pixels above, scipy.stats.kurtosis returns -0.21875 by default. Both conventions work as features, as long as all images use the same one.

One-pass formulas cancel large numbers

In the example, the four terms of the fourth moment are tens of millions, but the result is 445,000. Most of the value cancels, and rounding errors in the accumulated sums survive the subtraction. On the Matterhorn photo of (1,091,840 pixels, mean lightness 60.9), a simple loop that accumulates the four sums in 32-bit floating point gives a variance that is 0.39% too low and a kurtosis that is 3.2% too high. Three remedies help. Accumulate in 64-bit floating point: the relative errors then stay below 10-10. Subtract a rough estimate of the mean before accumulating, since the standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, and covariance do not change when all values shift: subtracting 85, the mean of the first ten rows, reduces the 32-bit errors below 0.05%. Or use update formulas that keep running central moments instead of raw sums; they are numerically stable and can also merge partial results computed in parallel (see Pébay in the Further Reading).

Fast Quadratic Distances¶

Let h\mathbf{h}h and g\mathbf{g}g be the normalized histograms of two images over NNN reference colors, so that the entries of each sum to 1. compares them with the quadratic distance, which takes the similarity between reference colors into account through a matrix A\mathbf{A}A. Its entries derive from the distances di,jd_{i,j}di,j​ between the reference colors cic_ici​ and cjc_jcj​:

δquad(h,g)=(h−g)⊤A (h−g),ai,j=1−di,jmax⁡k,ldk,l\delta_{\text{quad}}(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{g}) = (\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{g})^\top \mathbf{A}\, (\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{g}), \qquad a_{i,j} = 1 - \frac{d_{i,j}}{\max_{k,l} d_{k,l}}δquad​(h,g)=(h−g)⊤A(h−g),ai,j​=1−maxk,l​dk,l​di,j​​
(8)

Each comparison costs N2N^2N2 multiplications, against NNN for a Euclidean distance: 4096 for 64 reference colors, and a million for 1000. The index structures of Vector Search also expect a Euclidean or similar standard distance, not an arbitrary matrix. Both problems disappear if we can transform the histograms so that a Euclidean distance yields the same values.

The transformation uses the eigenvalue decomposition of A\mathbf{A}A. A symmetric matrix can be written as A=UΛU⊤\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\topA=UΛU⊤, where the columns ui\mathbf{u}_iui​ of U\mathbf{U}U are orthonormal eigenvectors and Λ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}Λ is the diagonal matrix of the eigenvalues λi\lambda_iλi​. If all eigenvalues are nonnegative, the matrix is positive semidefinite, and the square root Λ1/2\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}Λ1/2 exists. Splitting Λ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}Λ into two square roots gives

(h−g)⊤UΛ1/2 Λ1/2U⊤(h−g)=∥Λ1/2U⊤(h−g)∥2(\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{g})^\top \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top(\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{g}) = \lVert \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top(\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{g}) \rVert^2(h−g)⊤UΛ1/2Λ1/2U⊤(h−g)=∥Λ1/2U⊤(h−g)∥2
(9)

Distance and Similarity Measures shows the geometry of this rotation and scaling.

Key Formula: Quadratic Distance as a Euclidean Distance
h′=Λ1/2U⊤h,δquad(h,g)=∥h′−g′∥2=∑i=1Nλi(ui⊤(h−g))2\mathbf{h}' = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{h}, \qquad \delta_{\text{quad}}(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{g}) = \lVert \mathbf{h}' - \mathbf{g}' \rVert^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i \bigl(\mathbf{u}_i^\top(\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{g})\bigr)^2h′=Λ1/2U⊤h,δquad​(h,g)=∥h′−g′∥2=i=1∑N​λi​(ui⊤​(h−g))2
(10)

Condition: A\mathbf{A}A is symmetric and positive semidefinite, that is, λi≥0\lambda_i \ge 0λi​≥0 for all iii. The transformation rotates the histogram into the axes of the eigenvectors and stretches each axis by λi\sqrt{\lambda_i}λi​​. Every histogram is transformed once when it is indexed; at query time, a plain squared Euclidean distance replaces the matrix product.

Example

A=(10.7130.0990.713100.09901)\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.713 & 0.099 \\ 0.713 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.099 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}A=⎝⎛​10.7130.099​0.71310​0.09901​⎠⎞​
(11)

The eigenvalues are 0.2802, 1, and 1.7198, all positive. The eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue is u1=(0.7071,−0.7004,−0.0972)\mathbf{u}_1 = (0.7071, -0.7004, -0.0972)u1​=(0.7071,−0.7004,−0.0972): it contrasts sky blue with pale blue. The second, u2=(0,−0.1375,0.9905)\mathbf{u}_2 = (0, -0.1375, 0.9905)u2​=(0,−0.1375,0.9905), is almost pure dark green, and the third, u3=(0.7071,0.7004,0.0972)\mathbf{u}_3 = (0.7071, 0.7004, 0.0972)u3​=(0.7071,0.7004,0.0972), combines the two blues.

The query photo h=(0.6,0,0.4)\mathbf{h} = (0.6, 0, 0.4)h=(0.6,0,0.4), the hazy photo g=(0,0.6,0.4)\mathbf{g} = (0, 0.6, 0.4)g=(0,0.6,0.4), and the forest photo k=(0.2,0,0.8)\mathbf{k} = (0.2, 0, 0.8)k=(0.2,0,0.8) map to

h′=(0.2040,0.3962,0.6074),g′=(−0.2430,0.3137,0.6021),k′=(0.0337,0.7924,0.2875)\mathbf{h}' = (0.2040, 0.3962, 0.6074), \quad \mathbf{g}' = (-0.2430, 0.3137, 0.6021), \quad \mathbf{k}' = (0.0337, 0.7924, 0.2875)h′=(0.2040,0.3962,0.6074),g′=(−0.2430,0.3137,0.6021),k′=(0.0337,0.7924,0.2875)
(12)

The squared Euclidean distances between the transformed vectors are ∥h′−g′∥2=0.207\lVert \mathbf{h}' - \mathbf{g}' \rVert^2 = 0.207∥h′−g′∥2=0.207 and ∥h′−k′∥2=0.288\lVert \mathbf{h}' - \mathbf{k}' \rVert^2 = 0.288∥h′−k′∥2=0.288, the same values as the quadratic distances of the main text. Of the first distance, 0.200 lies on the first axis, the one with the smallest eigenvalue: moving pixels between sky blue and pale blue is cheap.

The transformed coordinates also give a fast filter step. Because every term λi(ui⊤(h−g))2\lambda_i (\mathbf{u}_i^\top(\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{g}))^2λi​(ui⊤​(h−g))2 is nonnegative, dropping some axes can only reduce the sum, so a distance over the axes with the largest eigenvalues is a lower bound of the full distance. A search can compute this short distance for all candidates, discard those whose lower bound already exceeds the current best, and compute the full distance only for the rest, without ever discarding a true neighbor. The bound can be loose, though. Keeping the two largest eigenvalues in the example gives 0.259 for the forest photo (true value 0.288) but only 0.007 for the hazy photo (true value 0.207), because h−g\mathbf{h} - \mathbf{g}h−g lies almost entirely on the dropped axis.

When the Matrix Is Not Positive Semidefinite¶

The construction ai,j=1−di,j/max⁡da_{i,j} = 1 - d_{i,j}/\max dai,j​=1−di,j​/maxd makes A\mathbf{A}A symmetric, but it does not guarantee nonnegative eigenvalues. With three reference colors and any distance that satisfies the triangle inequality, A\mathbf{A}A is always positive semidefinite, as in the example above; the problem appears with larger palettes. Take seven reference colors in RGB with channels scaled to [0,1][0, 1][0,1]: a mid gray (0.5,0.5,0.5)(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)(0.5,0.5,0.5) and the six colors that differ from it by 0.5 in exactly one channel, up or down. Under the Manhattan distance, a common way to combine the hue angle difference with the other channel differences in HSV, each outer color lies at distance 0.5 from the gray and at distance 1 from every other outer color. The matrix has 1 on the diagonal, 0.5 between the gray and each outer color, and 0 between outer colors. Its smallest eigenvalue is 1−0.56=−0.22471 - 0.5\sqrt{6} = -0.22471−0.56​=−0.2247, so λ\sqrt{\lambda}λ​ does not exist for this axis.

The negative eigenvalue has a visible effect on unnormalized counts. For h=(3,0,0,0,0,0,0)\mathbf{h} = (3, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)h=(3,0,0,0,0,0,0), three gray pixels, and g=(0,1,1,1,1,1,1)\mathbf{g} = (0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)g=(0,1,1,1,1,1,1), one pixel of each outer color, the “distance” is δquad(h,g)=−3\delta_{\text{quad}}(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{g}) = -3δquad​(h,g)=−3. After normalization, the same two histograms have the distance 0.1667. The difference of two normalized histograms always sums to zero, and on such vectors this matrix stays nonnegative. This holds in general for Euclidean and Manhattan ground distances: for these distances, x⊤A x≥0\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} \ge 0x⊤Ax≥0 for every x\mathbf{x}x whose entries sum to zero. The distance values are therefore fine, but the transformation still needs a square root of every eigenvalue. Three remedies exist:

  1. Center the matrix. Replace A\mathbf{A}A by Ac=PAP\mathbf{A}_c = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}Ac​=PAP with P=I−1N11⊤\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I} - \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\topP=I−N1​11⊤. For differences of normalized histograms, Ac\mathbf{A}_cAc​ yields exactly the same distances as A\mathbf{A}A, and for Euclidean and Manhattan ground distances it is positive semidefinite. For the seven colors, its eigenvalues are 0, 0.1429, and five times 1. The eigenvalue 0 belongs to the constant direction 1\mathbf{1}1, which differences of normalized histograms never use, so the transformed vectors need only N−1N-1N−1 coordinates.

  2. Use a kernel that is positive semidefinite by construction. With Euclidean distances, the Gaussian weights ai,j=exp⁡(−di,j2/(2s2))a_{i,j} = \exp(-d_{i,j}^2 / (2s^2))ai,j​=exp(−di,j2​/(2s2)) with a width sss give a positive definite matrix for every set of distinct reference colors. For the seven colors with s=0.5s = 0.5s=0.5, the smallest eigenvalue is 0.1144. The weights then decrease smoothly with the color distance instead of linearly.

  3. Clip negative eigenvalues to zero. This is the simplest fix, but it changes all distances, not only the problematic ones. For the seven colors, the distance between the two normalized histograms grows from 0.1667 to 0.3895.

Check the eigenvalues before transforming

A numerical library returns the eigenvalues of any symmetric matrix without complaint. A negative eigenvalue goes unnoticed until its square root turns into “not a number” or a distance becomes negative. Compute the smallest eigenvalue once when A\mathbf{A}A is built, and choose one of the remedies above if it is negative.

Gradient Moments¶

The Sobel operator of assigns two values to every pixel: the gradient magnitude gmag(x,y)g_{\text{mag}}(x,y)gmag​(x,y) and the gradient direction gdir(x,y)g_{\text{dir}}(x,y)gdir​(x,y). The main text turns them into an edge density and a gradient histogram. Moments summarize the same two distributions more compactly. For X∈{mag,dir}X \in \{\text{mag}, \text{dir}\}X∈{mag,dir}:

μX=1NM∑x,ygX(x,y),σX2=1NM∑x,y(gX(x,y)−μX)2\mu_X = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y} g_X(x,y), \qquad \sigma_X^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\bigl(g_X(x,y)-\mu_X\bigr)^2μX​=NM1​x,y∑​gX​(x,y),σX2​=NM1​x,y∑​(gX​(x,y)−μX​)2
(13)
sX=1NM∑x,y(gX(x,y)−μXσX)3,kX=1NM∑x,y(gX(x,y)−μXσX)4s_X = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\left(\frac{g_X(x,y)-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right)^3, \qquad k_X = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\left(\frac{g_X(x,y)-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right)^4sX​=NM1​x,y∑​(σX​gX​(x,y)−μX​​)3,kX​=NM1​x,y∑​(σX​gX​(x,y)−μX​​)4
(14)
covmag,dir=1NM∑x,y(gmag(x,y)−μmag)(gdir(x,y)−μdir)\text{cov}_{\text{mag},\text{dir}} = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\bigl(g_{\text{mag}}(x,y)-\mu_{\text{mag}}\bigr)\bigl(g_{\text{dir}}(x,y)-\mu_{\text{dir}}\bigr)covmag,dir​=NM1​x,y∑​(gmag​(x,y)−μmag​)(gdir​(x,y)−μdir​)
(15)

Four moments for each quantity and one covariance give nine values that describe the gradient distribution. The mean magnitude measures how much edge energy the image contains. Its skewness is large when most of the image is flat and a few strong edges stand out. The moments of the direction show whether edges prefer certain directions. All nine values can be computed in one pass with the formulas of the previous subsection.

The gradient direction is an angle

Two gradients at 179∘179^\circ179∘ and −179∘-179^\circ−179∘ point almost the same way, yet their linear mean is 0∘0^\circ0∘, the opposite direction. Their circular mean, atan2⁡(sin⁡α‾,cos⁡α‾)\operatorname{atan2}(\overline{\sin\alpha}, \overline{\cos\alpha})atan2(sinα,cosα) with the bars denoting averages, is 180∘180^\circ180∘ as expected. Moments of the raw angle therefore depend on where the angle range starts. Robust alternatives compute the moments of cos⁡gdir\cos g_{\text{dir}}cosgdir​ and sin⁡gdir\sin g_{\text{dir}}singdir​, weight each direction by its magnitude, or, when dark-to-light and light-to-dark edges should count the same, double the angle before averaging. The covariance between magnitude and direction inherits the same problem.

Laws’ Texture Energy¶

Kenneth Laws described texture with a small set of 5×55 \times 55×5 masks that can be applied to every pixel. The masks derive from four one-dimensional prototype vectors:

vL5=(1,4,6,4,1),vE5=(−1,−2,0,2,1),vS5=(−1,0,2,0,−1),vR5=(1,−4,6,−4,1)\mathbf{v}_{L5} = (1, 4, 6, 4, 1), \quad \mathbf{v}_{E5} = (-1, -2, 0, 2, 1), \quad \mathbf{v}_{S5} = (-1, 0, 2, 0, -1), \quad \mathbf{v}_{R5} = (1, -4, 6, -4, 1)vL5​=(1,4,6,4,1),vE5​=(−1,−2,0,2,1),vS5​=(−1,0,2,0,−1),vR5​=(1,−4,6,−4,1)
(16)

  • L5 (level) computes a center-weighted local average, close to a Gaussian.

  • E5 (edge) is a smoothed derivative and responds to step edges.

  • S5 (spot) has the shape of a Laplacian of Gaussian and responds to small spots.

  • R5 (ripple) alternates in sign like a small Gabor pattern and responds to fine ripples, the highest frequencies the mask can represent.

The entries of E5, S5, and R5 sum to zero, so these vectors do not respond to regions of constant brightness.

Multiplying a column vector with a row vector gives a two-dimensional kernel. With the first vector running down the rows and the second across the columns, the kernel for E5L5 is

GE5L5=vE5⊤vL5=(−1−2021)(14641)=(−1−4−6−4−1−2−8−12−8−20000028128214641)\mathbf{G}_{E5L5} = \mathbf{v}_{E5}^\top \mathbf{v}_{L5} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 & 6 & 4 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -4 & -6 & -4 & -1 \\ -2 & -8 & -12 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 8 & 12 & 8 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 6 & 4 & 1 \end{pmatrix}GE5L5​=vE5⊤​vL5​=⎝⎛​−1−2021​⎠⎞​(1​4​6​4​1​)=⎝⎛​−1−2021​−4−8084​−6−120126​−4−8084​−1−2021​⎠⎞​
(17)

It smooths along each row and differentiates from top to bottom, so it responds to horizontal edges. Its transpose GL5E5\mathbf{G}_{L5E5}GL5E5​ responds to vertical edges. The four vectors yield 4×4=164 \times 4 = 164×4=16 kernels.

Laws’ method convolves the image with each kernel, takes the absolute value of the response, and sums it over a window around each pixel, for example 15 by 15 pixels. The result is one texture energy map per kernel:

eXY(x,y)=∑(x′,y′)∈W(x,y)∣(I∗GXY)(x′,y′)∣e_{XY}(x,y) = \sum_{(x',y') \in W(x,y)} \bigl| (I * \mathbf{G}_{XY})(x',y') \bigr|eXY​(x,y)=(x′,y′)∈W(x,y)∑​∣∣​(I∗GXY​)(x′,y′)∣∣​
(18)

Three steps reduce the 16 maps to 9:

  1. Drop L5L5. Its entries sum to 256, so it measures local brightness rather than texture. It can still serve to normalize the other energies for contrast.

  2. Combine the six symmetric pairs. A pair such as E5L5 and L5E5 measures the same structure in two orientations. Averaging the two energy maps, eE5L5/L5E5=(eE5L5+eL5E5)/2e_{E5L5/L5E5} = (e_{E5L5} + e_{L5E5})/2eE5L5/L5E5​=(eE5L5​+eL5E5​)/2, gives a measure that treats horizontal and vertical structures alike. The pairs are E5L5/L5E5, S5L5/L5S5, R5L5/L5R5, E5S5/S5E5, E5R5/R5E5, and S5R5/R5S5.

  3. Keep the three symmetric kernels E5E5, S5S5, and R5R5 as they are.

Of the 16 maps, 15 remain after the first step, and combining six pairs leaves 15−6=915 - 6 = 915−6=9 texture energy values ei(x,y)e_i(x,y)ei​(x,y), 1≤i≤91 \le i \le 91≤i≤9, per pixel.

Average the energy maps, not the kernels

It is tempting to average the two kernels of a pair, (GE5L5+GL5E5)/2(\mathbf{G}_{E5L5} + \mathbf{G}_{L5E5})/2(GE5L5​+GL5E5​)/2, and convolve only once. The result is a different filter. On a step edge of height 100 that runs from the top right to the bottom left, E5L5 and L5E5 both respond with 3500, and so does the averaged kernel. On an edge from the top left to the bottom right, E5L5 responds with -3500 and L5E5 with +3500: the averaged kernel returns 0 and misses the edge, while the average of the absolute responses is still 3500. Averaging kernels builds a detector for one diagonal; averaging energies treats both diagonals, and horizontal and vertical edges, symmetrically.

From the nine energy maps, we build features with the methods of the main text:

  • Histograms are possible but large. With four quantization levels per energy, the histogram has 49=262,1444^9 = 262{,}14449=262,144 bins, far too many for a meaningful feature. With two levels, it has 29=5122^9 = 51229=512 bins, which is manageable, but each energy is then only “low” or “high”, a coarse quantization.

  • Moments are more compact. Four moments for each of the nine maps give 9×4=369 \times 4 = 369×4=36 values, and the covariances of all (92)=36\binom{9}{2} = 36(29​)=36 pairs of maps add 36 more, for a feature vector of 72 dimensions.

Gabor Filters in Fourier Space¶

introduces the Gabor filter as a Gaussian window multiplied by a complex wave. We repeat its definition because the Fourier view below builds on it. With the coordinates rotated by the angle θ\thetaθ,

gλ,θ,ϕ,σ,γ(x,y)=exp⁡ ⁣(−xˉ2+γ2yˉ22σ2)exp⁡ ⁣(i(2πxˉλ+ϕ)),xˉ=xcos⁡θ+ysin⁡θyˉ=−xsin⁡θ+ycos⁡θg_{\lambda,\theta,\phi,\sigma,\gamma}(x,y) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\bar{x}^2 + \gamma^2\bar{y}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \exp\!\left(i\left(2\pi\frac{\bar{x}}{\lambda} + \phi\right)\right), \qquad \begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta \\ \bar{y} &= -x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta \end{aligned}gλ,θ,ϕ,σ,γ​(x,y)=exp(−2σ2xˉ2+γ2yˉ​2​)exp(i(2πλxˉ​+ϕ)),xˉyˉ​​=xcosθ+ysinθ=−xsinθ+ycosθ​
(19)

The wavelength λ\lambdaλ sets the frequency 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ of the sinusoid in cycles per pixel, θ\thetaθ its direction, and ϕ\phiϕ its phase. The standard deviation σ\sigmaσ sets the size of the Gaussian envelope and γ\gammaγ its aspect ratio. A filter bank combines several directions and scales, and the moments of the filtered images form the texture feature. This subsection shows how the filtering is computed in Fourier space and what the filters look like there.

The FFT Pipeline¶

The convolution theorem states that a convolution in image space becomes a pointwise multiplication in Fourier space: I∗g=F−1(F(I)⋅F(g))I * g = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\bigl(\mathcal{F}(I) \cdot \mathcal{F}(g)\bigr)I∗g=F−1(F(I)⋅F(g)). Figure 1 shows the resulting pipeline. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) turns the grayscale image into a complex array with a real and an imaginary component. We multiply this array element by element with the Fourier transform of the Gabor filter, and the inverse FFT returns the filtered image. The filtered image is complex as well; its magnitude measures how strongly the selected frequency and direction are present at each pixel. For a bank of filters, the forward FFT of the image is computed only once and shared by all filters.

To inspect a spectrum, we display log⁡(1+∣F(I)∣2)\log\bigl(1 + |\mathcal{F}(I)|^2\bigr)log(1+∣F(I)∣2), the logarithm of the energy per frequency, with the zero frequency shifted to the center. The logarithm compresses the large differences between the dominant low frequencies and the weak high ones.

What a Gabor Filter Looks Like in Fourier Space¶

The Fourier transform of a Gaussian is again a Gaussian, with inverse width. The complex sinusoid ei2πxˉ/λe^{i 2\pi \bar{x}/\lambda}ei2πxˉ/λ shifts this Gaussian away from the origin to the frequency 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ in the direction θ\thetaθ. Together:

Key Formula: Gabor Filter in Fourier Space
G(u,v)=2πσ2γ eiϕexp⁡ ⁣(−2π2σ2[(uˉ−1λ)2+vˉ2γ2]),uˉ=ucos⁡θ+vsin⁡θvˉ=−usin⁡θ+vcos⁡θG(u,v) = \frac{2\pi\sigma^2}{\gamma}\, e^{i\phi} \exp\!\left(-2\pi^2\sigma^2\left[\left(\bar{u} - \frac{1}{\lambda}\right)^2 + \frac{\bar{v}^2}{\gamma^2}\right]\right), \qquad \begin{aligned} \bar{u} &= u\cos\theta + v\sin\theta \\ \bar{v} &= -u\sin\theta + v\cos\theta \end{aligned}G(u,v)=γ2πσ2​eiϕexp(−2π2σ2[(uˉ−λ1​)2+γ2vˉ2​]),uˉvˉ​=ucosθ+vsinθ=−usinθ+vcosθ​
(20)

In Fourier space, a Gabor filter is a single Gaussian blob centered at distance 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ from the origin in direction θ\thetaθ. Its width is 1/(2πσ)1/(2\pi\sigma)1/(2πσ) along that direction and γ/(2πσ)\gamma/(2\pi\sigma)γ/(2πσ) across it: the wider the filter in image space, the narrower its blob in Fourier space.

Example

A filter with λ=8\lambda = 8λ=8, θ=30∘\theta = 30^\circθ=30∘, σ=4\sigma = 4σ=4, and γ=0.5\gamma = 0.5γ=0.5 should have its blob at u=cos⁡30∘/8=0.1083u = \cos 30^\circ / 8 = 0.1083u=cos30∘/8=0.1083 and v=sin⁡30∘/8=0.0625v = \sin 30^\circ / 8 = 0.0625v=sin30∘/8=0.0625 cycles per pixel, with widths 1/(2π⋅4)=0.03981/(2\pi \cdot 4) = 0.03981/(2π⋅4)=0.0398 along the direction θ\thetaθ and 0.5/(2π⋅4)=0.01990.5/(2\pi \cdot 4) = 0.01990.5/(2π⋅4)=0.0199 across it. The FFT of the sampled kernel on a 256 by 256 grid has its maximum at u=0.1094u = 0.1094u=0.1094, v=0.0625v = 0.0625v=0.0625, the frequency bin closest to the prediction (bins are 1/256=0.00391/256 = 0.00391/256=0.0039 apart). The measured widths of the blob are 0.0398 and 0.0199, as predicted. A real-valued kernel that keeps only the cosine part of the filter has two blobs, at ±(0.1094,0.0625)\pm(0.1094, 0.0625)±(0.1094,0.0625), because the cosine is the sum of two complex exponentials with opposite frequencies.

The formula explains the layout of a filter bank in Fourier space, shown on the right of Figure %s. Each direction places its blobs along one ray from the center, and each scale places them on one ring. Directions only need to cover half a circle, θk=kπ/K\theta_k = k\pi/Kθk​=kπ/K for k=0,…,K−1k = 0, \ldots, K-1k=0,…,K−1. For phase ϕ=0\phi = 0ϕ=0, the filter for θ+π\theta + \piθ+π is the complex conjugate of the filter for θ\thetaθ, and the phase only rotates the complex response as a whole. On a real image, both directions therefore give responses of the same magnitude. Scales are usually spaced by a factor of two in frequency, with σ\sigmaσ growing in proportion to λ\lambdaλ so that every blob covers the same relative band. With λ=4,8,16\lambda = 4, 8, 16λ=4,8,16 and σ=λ/2\sigma = \lambda/2σ=λ/2, the blobs lie on rings of radius 0.25, 0.125, and 0.0625 cycles per pixel, with widths 0.080, 0.040, and 0.020 along the ray. High-frequency filters therefore appear as large blobs far from the center, and low-frequency filters as small blobs close to it. The typical frequencies of , between about 0.05 and 0.5 cycles per pixel, end at the Nyquist limit: a pattern that alternates every pixel is the finest one that pixels can represent. A bank with 6 directions and 3 scales, for example, has 18 filters.

Reading the Examples¶

A straight, high-contrast edge concentrates its energy along a line through the center of the spectrum, perpendicular to the edge. In the windsurfer photo of Figure %s, the mast against the white foam creates such a spike. The three filters whose blobs lie on this spike show the mast; the filter with a different direction misses it.

Figure 2 applies four filters with the same directions and scales to a mountain photo. The spectrum at the bottom left shows bright streaks through the center, produced by the ridge lines. Each filter selects a blob in this spectrum, and the inverse FFT shows where in the image the selected frequencies occur. Scale 3, the lowest frequency, responds with broad blobs in the clouds and along the horizon. Scales 2 and 1 respond to increasingly thin structures along the mountain contour. Direction 4 at scale 1 picks up different segments of the contour than direction 2, because the ridges on the two sides of the summit run in different directions.

FFT Sizes and Padding¶

FFT libraries such as FFTW and the FFTs in NumPy and SciPy handle images of any size in O(nlog⁡n)O(n \log n)O(nlogn) time, not only sizes that are powers of two. They are fastest when the size has only small prime factors such as 2, 3, 5, and 7, and slowest for large primes. In a measurement with SciPy, a 1000 by 1000 FFT (1000=23⋅531000 = 2^3 \cdot 5^31000=23⋅53) took 10.7 ms and a 1024 by 1024 FFT 10.5 ms, while a 1009 by 1009 FFT (1009 is prime) took 56.6 ms, about five times longer. The Matterhorn photo of has 853 rows, also a prime number; scipy.fft.next_fast_len(853) suggests padding to 864=25⋅33864 = 2^5 \cdot 3^3864=25⋅33 rows. Padding is the right adjustment; resizing would change the image and its frequencies.

Padding matters for a second reason. The discrete Fourier transform treats the image as periodic, as if its right border continued with its left border and its bottom with its top. The product of two spectra therefore computes a circular convolution, in which a filter near the border reaches across to the opposite side. For an ordinary convolution with a K×KK \times KK×K kernel, we pad the image with at least K−1K - 1K−1 additional rows and columns. On a 400 by 600 crop of the Matterhorn photo, filtering with a 31 by 31 Gabor kernel without padding produces errors of up to 3229 in the first 30 rows and columns, more than the largest correct response in the crop (2849). Away from these borders, the result agrees with direct convolution to within 10-11, and with padding to 430 by 630 it agrees everywhere. Zero padding creates an artificial edge at the image border; padding with a mirrored copy of the image avoids it.

Spatial Convolution or FFT¶

A Gabor filter can be applied in two ways: directly in image space, by sliding the kernel over the image and computing a weighted sum at every pixel as in , or in Fourier space with the FFT pipeline above. Both are practical, and their costs grow differently. A direct convolution with a K×KK \times KK×K kernel costs K2K^2K2 multiply-adds per pixel and filter, so its cost grows with the kernel. The FFT costs a few operations per pixel that grow only with the logarithm of the image size, independent of the kernel. On the full 853 by 1280 Matterhorn photo with a 31 by 31 kernel, SciPy’s direct convolution took 2.0 seconds and its FFT-based convolution 0.06 seconds. OpenCV’s filter2D took 0.016 seconds, because it switches to a DFT-based algorithm for kernels of about 11 by 11 pixels or larger and uses direct convolution for smaller ones. For small kernels, direct convolution is faster. In practice, we can leave the choice to the library: filter2D in OpenCV and scipy.signal.convolve with its default method="auto" both pick an algorithm.

The libraries differ in what they return. OpenCV’s getGaborKernel returns a real kernel, the real part of the filter with phase psi. The default phase is π/2\pi/2π/2, which gives an odd, sine-shaped kernel. To obtain the magnitude of the complex response, we filter with two kernels of phase 0 and π/2\pi/2π/2 and combine the two results r0r_0r0​ and rπ/2r_{\pi/2}rπ/2​ as r02+rπ/22\sqrt{r_0^2 + r_{\pi/2}^2}r02​+rπ/22​​. scikit-image’s skimage.filters.gabor returns the real and imaginary responses directly; it describes the filter by its frequency and bandwidth instead of λ\lambdaλ and σ\sigmaσ.

From Filtered Images to Features¶

After filtering, we summarize each filtered image with histograms or moments. With many filters, moments are preferred: they keep the feature short and avoid the quadratic distance over very large histograms. Let f~i(x,y)\tilde{f}_i(x,y)f~​i​(x,y) be the complex output of the iii-th filter. We treat the magnitudes ∣f~i(x,y)∣|\tilde{f}_i(x,y)|∣f~​i​(x,y)∣ as data points and compute their mean μi\mu_iμi​, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis, in one pass if we like. The covariance between two filters iii and jjj multiplies the two deviations:

covi,j=1NM∑x,y(∣f~i(x,y)∣−μi)(∣f~j(x,y)∣−μj)\text{cov}_{i,j} = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{x,y}\bigl(|\tilde{f}_i(x,y)| - \mu_i\bigr)\bigl(|\tilde{f}_j(x,y)| - \mu_j\bigr)covi,j​=NM1​x,y∑​(∣f~​i​(x,y)∣−μi​)(∣f~​j​(x,y)∣−μj​)
(21)

For a bank of 15 filters, these moments and covariances form the 165-value feature of the example in .
